question: Which CFS section includes purchase of a new factory?
before: Capex (new factory) is in Cash Flow from Investing Activities as an outflow. Not operational (long-term investment). Not financing (asset acquisition not capital structure).
after:
Concept: The Cash Flow Statement divides all cash movements into three sections based on their nature: Operating Activities (day-to-day business), Investing Activities (purchase and sale of long-term assets), and Financing Activities (debt and equity capital structure changes).

Why this is correct: Purchase of a new factory is a capital expenditure (Capex) — an acquisition of a long-term productive asset. By definition, all Capex belongs in the Investing Activities section of the CFS, shown as a cash outflow.

Why the others are wrong: Option A (Operating Activities) is incorrect because operating activities cover routine cash flows from running the business (sales, expenses, payroll), not one-time asset purchases. Option C (Financing Activities) is incorrect because financing activities involve raising or repaying capital (debt issuance, equity issuance, dividends), not acquiring assets. Option D (Not on the CFS) is incorrect because Capex is explicitly required to appear on the CFS; it is a material cash outflow that must be reported.

Intuition: A factory is a building block of long-term production capacity, not part of this year's profit-and-loss operations. Equity analysts use the Investing Activities section to assess management's capital allocation discipline — large, recurring Capex signals growth ambitions or maintenance needs, while low or declining Capex may signal contraction or underinvestment.
